questions.prompt: A repository holds one commit, S, on main. Someone runs: git switch -c draft, commits D1, runs git switch main, and commits M1. How many commits does main reach now?
options: 3: S, D1 and M1
2: S and M1
1: M1 only
4: S twice, D1 and M1
questions.explanation: Main reaches its own commit M1 and the parent chain back to S; D1 is reachable from draft only.
misconceptions: Counts every commit made in the repository as part of main
Thinks a commit replaces its parent instead of pointing to it
Believes a branch copies the commits it starts from

questions.prompt: Main has not moved since the branch topic was created; topic now has two commits. On main you run git merge topic. What does the graph show afterwards?
options: A new merge commit with two parents on main
Copies of the two topic commits, with new ids, on main
Main moves to the last commit of topic; no new commit
Topic deleted, its commits now belonging to main
questions.explanation: When main is an ancestor of topic, Git only moves the main pointer forward: a fast-forward.
misconceptions: Expects a merge commit even when one side has not moved
Confuses a merge with a rebase that rewrites commits
Thinks commits belong to a branch rather than branches pointing at commits

questions.prompt: git commit -am "message" also commits a new file that git does not track yet.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The -a flag stages changes to files git already tracks; a new file needs git add first.
misconceptions: Thinks -a means every file in the folder

questions.prompt: A teammate pushed two commits to the hub. You run git fetch and nothing else. What has changed in your clone?
options: Your main now includes the two new commits
Your working files changed to the hub's version
Nothing, because fetch only lists what is new
origin/main moved; your own main did not
questions.explanation: Fetch downloads the commits and moves the remote-tracking names; merging them into main is a separate step.
misconceptions: Takes fetch for pull: fetch never moves your own branches
Thinks fetching rewrites the working folder
Believes fetch is read-only reporting; it downloads commits and moves origin/ names

questions.prompt: A ticket log has the agent code in field 3, fields separated by spaces. Which pipeline counts tickets per agent?
options: cut -d' ' -f3 tickets.log | sort | uniq -c
cut -d' ' -f3 tickets.log | uniq -c | sort
sort tickets.log | uniq -c | cut -d' ' -f3
cut -d' ' -f3 tickets.log | wc -l
questions.explanation: Keep the field, sort so equal codes sit together, then count each run.
misconceptions: Forgets that uniq only merges neighbouring equal lines
Counts whole lines before keeping the field, so every line is unique
Counts all lines at once instead of per agent

questions.prompt: Without set -o pipefail, the exit code of a pipeline is the exit code of its last command.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Bash reports the last command's status unless pipefail asks for the last non-zero one.
misconceptions: Believes any failing stage makes the whole pipeline fail by default

questions.prompt: A script writes its results to standard output and its warnings to standard error. Which command keeps the results in out.txt and the warnings in err.txt?
options: bash tally.sh > out.txt > err.txt
bash tally.sh 2> out.txt > err.txt
bash tally.sh > out.txt 2> err.txt
bash tally.sh | tee out.txt err.txt
questions.explanation: > redirects standard output (1) and 2> standard error; each goes to its own file.
misconceptions: Thinks a second > sends the second stream; both redirect standard output
Swaps the stream numbers: 2 is standard error
Expects a pipe to carry standard error too

questions.prompt: A folder is named site photos, with a space. Which command lists its files?
options: ls site photos
ls site\photos
ls 'site' photos
ls "site photos"
questions.explanation: Quotes keep the name one word, so ls receives a single argument.
misconceptions: Forgets that the shell splits unquoted words on spaces
Puts the backslash before the wrong character: it must escape the space
Quotes one word only, so the shell still sees two arguments

questions.prompt: A pull request changes how the report counts alert hours. Which review comment helps the author most?
options: Line 40: 150 is also in rules.md; read it from one place
Looks fine to me, approved without further comments
I would have done this differently, but it is your call
Please rewrite the whole module in a cleaner, more modern style
questions.explanation: A useful comment names the line, the problem and a way forward, and stays inside the request.
misconceptions: Approves without reading, so the reviewer adds nothing
Gives an opinion with no line, no reason and no suggestion
Asks for a change far beyond the request, with no concrete point

questions.prompt: You commit a fix on main and run git push. The host answers that main is protected. What is the normal next step?
options: Push again with --force to override the check
Push it on a branch and open a pull request
Ask the host administrator to lift the protection
Delete the local commit and wait for a reviewer
questions.explanation: Protection means main changes only through a reviewed request; the commit itself is fine on a branch.
misconceptions: Thinks force overrides the host's branch protection
Treats the protection as an obstacle rather than the team's review rule
Believes the change itself is refused, when only the route is

questions.prompt: When a pull request no longer merges cleanly, its author usually brings the current main into the branch, resolves the conflict there, and pushes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The author knows the change best; resolving on the branch keeps main clean and lets the reviewer see the resolution.
misconceptions: Thinks the reviewer or the host resolves conflicts at merge time

questions.prompt: A commit that set a wrong threshold was pushed yesterday and others have pulled it. How do you undo it?
options: git reset --hard to the commit before it, then force-push
git commit --amend to change it
git revert with that commit's id, then push
git restore on the file, without a commit
questions.explanation: Revert records a new commit that reverses the old one, so nobody's history is rewritten.
misconceptions: Rewrites history others already have, so their clones disagree
Amend only changes the last local commit, and still rewrites it
Changes the working file only; history and the hub stay wrong

questions.prompt: A project declares tabulate>=0.9 in pyproject.toml. What does its lock file add?
options: Nothing more, since the declaration already names the package
A copy of each package's source code
The versions of the direct packages only
Exact versions and hashes of all packages, indirect ones too
questions.explanation: The declaration says what is acceptable; the lock records exactly what was resolved, down to indirect dependencies and hashes.
misconceptions: Takes a lower bound for a fixed version
Confuses the lock with a vendored copy of the packages
Forgets the packages those packages need

questions.prompt: uv sync --locked stops with an error that the lockfile needs to be updated. What does that mean, and what do you do?
options: The declaration changed after the lock: run uv lock, commit both
The package index is unreachable from this network: retry it later
The lock is corrupt: delete it and run without it
A package was removed from the index: pin an older one
questions.explanation: --locked refuses to change the lock; the fix is to update it on purpose and commit it with the declaration.
misconceptions: Reads a mismatch between two files as a connection problem
Throws away the record that makes the rebuild repeatable
Guesses at a cause the message does not state

questions.prompt: A container on a Linux host uses the host's kernel; it is an isolated process, not a separate machine.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Containers share the host kernel, which is why a kernel flaw or a mounted folder reaches across.
misconceptions: Believes a container is a small virtual machine with its own kernel

questions.prompt: A report image reads its input from /data and writes to /out. Which run keeps the input safe from the program?
options: run -v ./data:/data -v ./output:/out report
run -v ./data:/data:ro -v ./output:/out report
run -v ./data:/out:ro -v ./output:/data report
run report, with the data copied into the image
questions.explanation: A read-only bind mount gives the program the data without letting it change it; the output folder is writable.
misconceptions: Leaves the input writable, so a bug can change the raw data
Swaps the folders: the program would write into the input
Bakes data into the image, so each month needs a new image

questions.prompt: A scan finds a live API key in a commit from last month. What do you do first?
options: Rewrite the history so that no commit holds the key any more
Delete the file in a new commit
Revoke or rotate the key at the service that issued it
Make the repository private
questions.explanation: Until the key is revoked, anyone with an old copy can use it; cleaning history comes second.
misconceptions: Cleans the repository while the key still works for anyone who copied it
Removes it from the latest version only; the old commit still holds it
Hides it from new readers, not from those who already cloned it

questions.prompt: Removing the settings file that held a key, in a new commit, removes the key from the repository.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Every earlier commit still holds the file; git log -S finds it until the history is rewritten.
misconceptions: Thinks a repository holds only its latest version

questions.prompt: A project needs a key. Which set-up keeps it out of the repository and still tells a newcomer what to provide?
options: The key in settings.toml, and settings.toml added to .gitignore afterwards
The key base64-encoded in the code
The key in the README, in a section marked private
An ignored .env file, and a committed .env.example naming the variable
questions.explanation: The value lives only in an ignored file or the environment; the example file documents the name.
misconceptions: Ignoring a file already committed does not untrack it, and nothing documents the name
Takes encoding for encryption: anyone can decode it
Puts the secret in the most-read file of the repository

questions.prompt: A history was rewritten to remove a key and force-pushed. What must everyone who cloned it before do?
options: Clone again, or reset hard to the rewritten branch
Nothing, because the next git pull fixes their copy
Run the secret scanner once
Commit their work and push it to the hub as usual
questions.explanation: Rewritten commits have new ids; old clones still hold the old commits and must be replaced.
misconceptions: A pull merges the old history back, key included
Scanning finds the key but does not remove it from their copy
Pushing an old-history branch brings the removed commits back

questions.prompt: Which Reproduce section lets a peer rebuild a report project on a clean machine?
options: Run the notebook top to bottom
Tools needed, where to get the data, one rebuild command and the expected checksum
See the code for details
Contact the analyst for the data path
questions.explanation: A peer needs the prerequisites, the data source, one command and a way to tell success from failure.
misconceptions: Assumes the peer has the same packages, data and folder
Leaves every decision to the reader
Makes reproduction depend on one person being available

questions.prompt: In a peer reproduction, the rebuild fails: no such folder data/. The repository rightly does not hold the data. What is the fix?
options: Commit the data folder into the repository so that every clone has it
Tell the peer the folder in a chat message
State where the data comes from and read its folder from a variable
Hard-code the peer's folder in the script
questions.explanation: The README carries the knowledge; the script takes the location from outside.
misconceptions: Puts data back into the code repository
Fixes this run only; the next reader hits the same wall
Ties the script to a second computer instead of the first

questions.prompt: If a fresh clone rebuilds correctly on the author's own laptop, a peer reproduction adds nothing.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The author's laptop still holds caches, tools and knowledge the README may not state; a peer on a clean workspace finds those gaps.
misconceptions: Equates a clean folder with a clean machine and a fresh reader

questions.prompt: How does a peer know a rebuild reproduced the expected result rather than just running?
options: The program prints no error
The output file exists in the output folder after the rebuild has run
The numbers look plausible
The rebuild compares the output with a committed checksum
questions.explanation: A committed checksum turns "it ran" into "it produced the same bytes".
misconceptions: Takes running without error for being right
Checks presence, not content
Relies on judgement where an exact check is possible
